analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC money in House races, caps House campaign spending, and reins in party soft money.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-backed bill to ban PAC contributions in House races and cap House campaign spending died in committee without a hearing or a vote as the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten how House members raise money. It banned House candidates from taking any money from political action committees and from anyone outside their own district, put a $600,000 cap on campaign spending and contributions, and required candidates who accepted those caps to report opponents who tried to spend around them. It also forced political party 'soft money' — unregulated contributions funneled through state party committees — under the same contribution limits and disclosure rules as other campaign money, and banned the use of government aircraft in federal campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would see House campaigns funded by their own district's residents instead of out-of-district PACs and big donors; and future House candidates who agree to spending limits, who would get a more even playing field against big-money opponents.

how_it_helps.text: Bars House candidates from accepting contributions from multicandidate political committees (PACs) or from any source other than individuals, and limits contributions to individual residents of the candidate's congressional district [S2] [S3].
Caps an eligible House candidate's expenditures and contributions at $600,000 per election cycle, with $500,000 of that in the general election period, indexed to inflation [S2] [S3].

Protects candidates who accept the caps: if a non-participating opponent spends more than 80 percent of the general election limit or raises more than 50 percent of it, the limits no longer bind the capped candidate [S3].

Subjects all money solicited, received, or spent by national, state, and local party committees in connection with federal elections — including soft money — to the contribution limits, prohibitions, and reporting requirements of federal law, and bars national party committees from soliciting contributions outside those limits [S2] [S3].
Requires party committees to report all receipts and disbursements during federal election periods, whether or not connected to a federal election [S3].

Bans use of government-owned or operated aircraft in connection with federal elections, with the President and Vice President's campaigns required to repay the campaign-related share of their travel costs [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees and their corporate and union sponsors, big out-of-district donors, and the House incumbents whose campaigns those contributions fund; party committees lose the soft money channel and face new spending caps and reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, big donors, and party committees

drawbacks.text: The spending and contribution caps only apply to candidates who agree to them, and a rival who opts out and crosses the spending or fundraising thresholds frees the capped candidate from the limits — a design that gives well-funded candidates a way to pressure opponents out of the voluntary system [S3].

Restricting contributions to district residents only could starve challengers in expensive media markets of fundraising reach while favoring incumbents with local networks; general experience with mandatory expenditure limits also raises constitutional questions the courts had already narrowed by the time this was introduced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core exchange is strong for voters: it replaces PAC and out-of-district money with contributions from the people a House member actually represents, and pulls unregulated party soft money under disclosure and limits. The weaknesses are real but modest: the limits are voluntary and escape clauses let big-spending opponents break the cap, and a district-only rule could make it harder for underfunded challengers to raise money quickly. On balance the bill is a genuine anti-corruption reform with an enforceable, if leaky, design — the kind of bill sitting members had little incentive to advance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote there, and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry Costello, a Democrat from Illinois, introduced the Campaign Finance System Reform Act in the House on May 19, 1992 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which handles election law [S5] [S1].
Two Republicans cosponsored the bill, making the initial sponsorship a small bipartisan group of three members [S4] [S1].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and the congressional record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote; the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the PACs, big donors, and party committees that fund them — the existing campaign money system, with its soft money channel and government-aircraft perks, carried into the next election untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent House members and their PAC funders

sides.party_line_note: Only three members sponsored the bill — one Democrat and two Republicans — and no vote was ever recorded, so the record never shows where the broader House stood.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, labor, and trade PACs)
industries.note: The bill would have cut PACs off entirely from House races, ending their role as a main channel of congressional campaign money. Their gain under the status quo — access purchased through contributions — is the public's cost in influence over House members.

The bill would have shut down the soft money channel by making all party money tied to federal elections subject to federal limits and disclosure, and capped party spending; it also gave individuals a slightly higher overall limit when giving to state parties. Parties kept a regulated role, but lost the unregulated money.

New definitions treat coordinated outside spending as a contribution subject to limits, and out-of-district individuals could no longer give to House candidates. Spending by outside groups would shrink or come under federal rules.
